authors.context: Nadere Reformatie; Utrecht pastor 1653–1677 (called 1652, installed April 1653)
notes: Do not treat all Uyt-spanningen entries as a uniform public-worship hymnbook.

Ministry dates: Zoetermeer 1644, Sluis 1650, Utrecht from April 1653 to 1677 — 2005 critical-edition introduction, p. 645, read 2026-10-25. Sources that give 1644, 1650 and 1653 are listing the three pastorates, not disagreeing.
I. and II. Hert-sterckte in Jehova are distinct poems: I on printed pp. 78-81 (28 December 1673), II on pp. 82-84 (4 January 1674), sung to I's tune.
In December 1673 he was held as a French hostage away from Utrecht; the four consolation songs of that exile were printed in 1674 as 'Meditatien over eenige van 's Heeren Gods Eygenschappen'.
For DUTCH-002, distinguish source author Lodenstein from Rutgers as later reviser.
Do not call the Russian adaptation a verbatim translation of the 1674 poem.
Hy droech onse smerten is a sonnet; the 1630 first edition is not independently acquired in this project.
No original tune direction is verified.

authors.canonicalName: Anonymous — the author of Φῶς ἱλαρόν
authors.context: Greek Christian hymn sung at the lighting of the lamps; already called ancient and anonymous by Basil of Caesarea c. 375
notes: Basil writes that he cannot say who composed the lamp-lighting thanksgiving; that is the earliest and the strongest statement about authorship.

Athenogenes of Sebasteia (m. c. 305/311) is named because Basil mentions his hymn in the next sentence; the two testimonies were conflated. Sophronius of Jerusalem (560-638) is the ascription printed in the modern Russian Horologion and is contradicted by P. Lond. 2037B.
Neither attribution may be stated in public copy as fact.
